nodes.question: What is a potential problem with ensiling cover crops?
nodes.answer: The potential problem is their relatively high moisture content at the time of harvest, which may cause issues for fermentation.
nodes.paragraph: 2017). A poten- tial problem with the ensiling of cover crops is their relatively high moisture content at the time of har - vest, which may cause problems for the fermentation. Such problems may be combated by co-ensiling cover crops with straw (Feng et al. 2019). To avoid losses of straw before the harvesting of cover crops and limit the number of field operations, the most viable strat- egy is to harvest the straw at the time of harvest of the main crop and store it until the cover crops also have been harvested (Fontaine et al. 2020a). Cover crops and other agricultural residues are not commonly used as exclusive feedstock in biogas plants (Feng et al. 2020; Thamsiriroj et al. 2012; Xie 215 Nutr Cycl Agroecosyst (2025) 130:213 232 Vol. : (123456789) et al. 2011). Common practice is to co-digest with animal manure (Feng et al. 2020). The implementa- tion of technology for anaerobic digestion of cover crops is thus most feasible at animal farms, where co- digestion with animal manure is possible.

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What is the hypothesized environmental benefit of digesting cover crops and cattle manure?
nodes.answer: The hypothesized environmental benefit is overall positive impacts on ecosystems and resource availability due to displacement of natural gas.
nodes.paragraph: This was compared to the mono-digestion of cattle manure and a baseline sce- nario of soil incorporation of residues, using agricul- tural modelling and consequential LCA. We hypoth- esize that digesting cover crops and cattle manure would result in overall benefits for the environment, including ecosystems and resource availability due to displacement of natural gas. Methods Goal and scope Definition of the system An example-farm of 1,0 hectares and 560 dairy cat- tle was modelled, under Danish conditions. The num- ber of cattle was decided based on the amount of feed that could be produced at 1,0 hectares (detailed data included in the Supplementary information (SI)). The assessment was focused on the management of residues at the farm, including the cattle manure and the cover crop- and straw residues, applying conse- quential LCA methodology (Brand o et al. 2022). The farm area was divided into two crop rotation systems of 500 hectares each (rotation 1 and 2), of which one was included in the LCA (Fig. 1). These 500 hectares were used for cultivation of spring bar - ley, with under-sown cover crops (rotation 1).

nodes.question: During which growth stages are N2O and N2 emissions highest?
nodes.answer: N2O and N2 emissions are highest during early growth stages, ripening, and after harvest, particularly when plant nitrogen and water uptake are low.
nodes.paragraph: Growing plants affected all controlling factors of denitrification, and dynamics clearly differed between crop species. Overall, N2O and N2 emissions were highest when plant N and water uptake were low, i.e., during early growth stages, ripening, and after harvest. We present the first dataset of a plot-scale field study employing the improved 15N gas flux method over a growing season showing that drivers for N2O and N2O + N2 fluxes differ between crop species and change throughout the growing season. Keywords Denitrification Nitrogen Cycling N balance Plant N uptake Crop development Introduction Denitrification is one of the main sources of gaseous N losses to the environment with N2O and N2 being its main end products. N2O is an important greenhouse gas with a global warming potential of 298-times that of CO2 (Ciais et al. 2014) and emissions of N2O from agriculture have been monitored for several decades. In contrast, N2 is inert, and there are very few studies directly measuring N2 emis- sions on the field scale.
